articles.title: The housing crisis is now global. It shows just how undemocratic our nations have become | Leilani Farha
articles.summary: When we can’t even afford to rent or buy somewhere to live, we have to ask: did we give the financial sector too much power? Leilani Farha is the former UN special rapporteur on adequate housing In the summer of 2021, I visited a homeless community in a park…
articles.content: When we can’t even afford to rent or buy somewhere to live, we have to ask: did we give the financial sector too much power? Leilani Farha is the former UN special rapporteur on adequate housing In the summer of 2021, I visited a homeless community in a park in Toronto, Canada, and spoke to one of the residents. He was living in a tent in the shadow of brand new skyscrapers, and had been homeless for about five years. At one point he swivelled around, pointed up at a crane on the skyline, and said: “Who are they building those for? Definitely not for me.” He was right. And he captured something experienced by ordinary people around the world: the growing conviction that the housing system is no longer tethered to their needs. What he was pointing at is not just a housing crisis. It is a crisis of democracy. Leilani Farha is the 2026 CBC Massey lecturer. This piece is based on her new book: Housing Inc.: A Global Takeover and Our Fight for Home . She is the former UN special rapporteur on adequate housing and the global director of the international human rights organisation, The Shift Continue reading...
articles.aiArticle:
The widespread inability of ordinary people to secure affordable shelter points to a deeper institutional failure, raising sharp questions about whether modern democracies have ceded excessive control to the financial sector, according to an opinion piece published by **Business | The Guardian**. Authored by **Leilani Farha**, the former UN special rapporteur on adequate housing, the commentary reflects on an encounter in the summer of **2021** with a homeless community residing in a park. This personal observation underpins the argument that skyrocketing property and rental costs are not merely market adjustments, but symptoms of a political system prioritizing financial interests over fundamental human needs.

## The Financialization of Shelter

According to the report, the transformation of housing into a traded commodity has severed the link between shelter and local wages. Farha argues that as institutional investors and global capital treat residential properties as speculative assets, communities face unprecedented displacement. This systemic shift often occurs while local and national leaders negotiate complex private agreements, echoing controversies such as the recent scrutiny surrounding the [Manchester City owner’s £55m housing loan while Burnham was mayor investigated](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/manchester-city-owner-s-m-housing-loan-while-burnham-was-mayor-investigated). Critics of current urban planning point out that these dynamics mirror broader economic strains, drawing parallels to how [‘Countries are defying gravity’: how much longer can global economy resist chaos?](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/countries-are-defying-gravity-how-much-longer-can-global-economy-resist-chaos) as policymakers struggle to balance growth with basic social welfare.

## Broader Context and Systemic Stakes

*Context: Housing affordability has emerged as a central flashpoint in contemporary politics across developed economies, frequently intersecting with monetary policy decisions made by central banks and global financial institutions. When shelter costs outpace income growth for prolonged periods, the social contract frays, deepening economic inequality and pushing younger generations out of the property market entirely. The core debate centers on whether governments retain the regulatory tools to subordinate financial market yields to the public good, or if housing will remain permanently bound to global capital flows.*

## What to Watch

Observers should monitor upcoming legislative proposals regarding foreign ownership limits and institutional landlord taxation, which could signal whether governments are willing to confront real estate financialization. Future policy debates will likely focus on whether courts and human rights tribunals begin recognizing adequate shelter as an enforceable legal guarantee rather than a market commodity.

articles.aiArticle:
Authorities on the remote Indian Ocean island of **Anjouan** are grappling with an illicit offshore gambling network allegedly tied to a London-based family of property investors, according to a report by **Business | The Guardian**. The tiny island, situated between Mozambique and Madagascar, has seen its name and supposed regulatory credentials hijacked by online casinos operating without local authorization. While investigators trace the digital operations back to British soil, the London property investors named in the inquiry have strenuously denied selling gambling licences. 

## The London Property Connection and Island Denials

According to the published findings, the network exploits the jurisdictional obscurity of Anjouan to project legitimacy to online gamblers across Europe and beyond. The London-based investors at the center of the controversy insist they have no involvement in issuing gaming permits or managing the rogue virtual betting platforms. Local officials on the island, meanwhile, maintain that the digital operations are entirely unauthorized, raising serious questions about how foreign actors manage to weaponize small island sovereignties for digital commerce. This illicit ecosystem mirrors broader concerns about digital exploitation seen elsewhere, similar to how [Gabon fights to protect sacred plant from US drug companies](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/the-next-ayahuasca-gabon-fights-to-protect-sacred-plant-from-us-graph) against corporate overreach.

## Why This Matters

Unregulated offshore gambling operations pose significant regulatory and financial risks, particularly when smaller island jurisdictions are used to mask the true origins of digital enterprises. For consumers, betting on sites that lack legitimate oversight means zero protection against fraud, withheld winnings, or rigged games. Furthermore, such illicit networks damage the international reputation and sovereignty of vulnerable territories like Anjouan, diverting potential legal revenues away from local populations while shifting liability onto communities unable to police international cyber networks. The situation underscores the immense challenges regulators face when trying to rein in borderless digital economies operated from major financial capitals.

## Regulatory Response and What to Watch

As scrutiny mounts over digital betting operations and corporate accountability, observers should monitor whether British regulatory bodies launch formal investigations into the property investors named in the report. Another key development to watch will be how island authorities in the Indian Ocean attempt to legally reclaim their jurisdiction and crack down on unauthorized entities using their geographical identity online. Residents living in the remote Arctic settlement of **Longyearbyen** on the Norwegian archipelago of **Svalbard** have been instructed that their tap water is no longer safe to drink, according to World news | The Guardian. The advisory was issued after climate-related thawing triggered the release of heavy metals into the municipal water supply. Situated in one of the fastest-warming regions on the planet, the community now faces a sudden public health challenge that experts warn could foreshadow similar crises for other settlements across the polar north. 

## Thawing Permafrost and Metal Contamination

The unfolding situation in Svalbard highlights the hidden vulnerabilities of infrastructure built upon permafrost that is rapidly degrading under rising global temperatures. According to the report, the warming climate has directly caused the thawing of surrounding terrain, which in turn mobilized heavy metals into the local water system. Local authorities acted swiftly to issue the warning to residents, though the abrupt loss of a reliable potable water source has left the population scrambling for alternatives. 

## Broader Implications for Arctic Settlements

While local crews work to address the contamination, the incident in Longyearbyen serves as a stark warning for other municipalities in high-latitude regions facing similar environmental shifts. Similar infrastructural stress points are emerging globally, comparable to how sudden municipal failures can disrupt daily life, such as the [stinky business in south London where a local bike shop was hit by an unbearable stench from a Thames Water sewer](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/stinky-business-south-london-bike-shop-hit-by-unbearable-stench-from-thames). As climate pressures mount, remote towns must reassess how their foundational utilities will withstand the physical consequences of a shifting ecosystem.

## Why This Matters

*Context:* The breakdown of basic municipal services in the high Arctic demonstrates the direct, tangible human costs of rapid environmental change. When essential resources like drinking water become compromised by thawing terrain, isolated communities face severe logistical hurdles to secure basic necessities. This vulnerability underscores the urgent need for climate adaptation strategies that go beyond emission reduction and actively fortify aging infrastructure against physical degradation.

## What to Watch

*Context:* Observers will be monitoring how Norwegian authorities manage the immediate logistical burden of supplying clean drinking water to the isolated population of Longyearbyen. Future updates are expected to focus on long-term remediation efforts and whether similar warnings will be issued for other vulnerable settlements across the Arctic.

articles.aiArticle:
British corporations listed on stock exchanges have hit a two-year high in profit warnings, according to a recent report from **Business | The Guardian**. The consultancy-tracked data reveals that firms quoted on the London market issued **65** warnings during the three months leading up to the end of September. This sharp increase stems directly from the escalating conflict in the Middle East, which has sparked a dramatic surge in operational expenses for businesses across the country. 

## Escalating Conflict Triggers Corporate Strain

The mounting financial pressure on British enterprises is largely driven by external geopolitical shocks, as the war involving Iran pushes operational expenses upward. According to the report, corporate leaders are struggling to absorb the sudden escalation in overhead, forcing them to adjust their financial forecasts downward. These developments echo broader industrial struggles across the nation, similar to how high [electricity costs put UK steelmakers in worst position in three years against EU rivals](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/electricity-costs-put-uk-steelmakers-in-worst-position-in-three-years-against), compounding the manufacturing sector's woes.

## The Broader Economic Context

Corporate profit warnings serve as an early indicator of wider economic distress, signaling potential contractions in business investment and employment stability. When supply chains face severe disruption and energy or shipping expenses spike due to international conflicts, companies frequently find their profit margins squeezed before they can successfully pass those expenses on to consumers. 

*(Context: Profit warnings are formal announcements made by publicly traded companies to inform shareholders that their financial results will fall short of previous expectations. These alerts typically trigger an immediate sell-off in a company's shares as investors reevaluate its market value.)*

## Why This Matters

This spike in financial alerts affects everyday workers, investors, and the stability of domestic pension funds heavily invested in London-listed equities. When major corporations repeatedly downgrade their earnings, it dampens market confidence, curtails hiring initiatives, and limits corporate spending on vital infrastructure. The compounding effect of soaring overheads and fragile market demand places intense pressure on executive boards to restructure operations rapidly to avoid deeper financial distress.

## What to Watch

Observers will monitor whether the conflict in the Middle East continues to escalate, which would likely sustain upward pressure on global energy and transport expenses. Market analysts will also scrutinize upcoming quarterly corporate earnings reports to see which specific sectors are absorbing the heaviest losses and whether further downward revisions to financial forecasts are forthcoming.

Sources: [Business | The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/oct/19/profit-warnings-from-uk-listed-firms-at-highest-level-in-two-years-as-iran-war-drives-up-costs)
